entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Baldo Angelo Abati, a distinguished Italian physician and naturalist, flourished in the latter half of the sixteenth century, leaving a significant, albeit specialized, imprint on the burgeoning fields of natural history and pharmacology during the Renaissance. Operating within the intellectual currents of Early Modern Italy, Abati's work exemplified the era's blend of classical medical tradition, particularly Galenism, with an increasing drive for empirical observation and detailed categorization of the natural world. His associations with prominent patrons, notably Duke Guidobaldo II della Rovere of Urbino, underscore the interconnectedness of scientific inquiry and aristocratic sponsorship in this period.

Abati's principal contributions are encapsulated in two seminal works. His *De natura thermarum* (1572) stands as an exhaustive treatise on balneology, meticulously cataloging Italian thermal springs, analyzing their chemical compositions, and prescribing their therapeutic uses for a wide array of ailments. This work was crucial for standardizing the use of mineral waters in medicine. Perhaps more famously, his *De admirabili viperae natura et de mirificis eiusdem facultatibus* (1589) delved into the natural history of the viper, meticulously describing its anatomy, behavior, and, critically, its venom. Abati also explored the medicinal applications of viper flesh and venom, contributing to early pharmacological understanding and the development of theriac, a complex antidote.
